title: The differential impacts of markets for technology on the value of technological resources: An application of group‐based trajectory models
abstract: Research summary : This article uses Group‐Based Trajectory ( GBT ) Models to advance strategic management research, focusing on demonstrating the differential impacts of markets for technology on the value of technological capabilities. Group Based Trajectory ( GBT ) models, a statistical technique based on finite mixture models, can be used to discern heterogeneity based on an attribute of interest, especially when the heterogeneity changes or evolves over time, and when there is a lack of theoretical guidance to discern the basis of heterogeneity. We illustrate these advantages of GBT models in our study of how the moderating effect of markets for technology on the value of technological capability is itself moderated by firm types. We conclude with a discussion of potential uses of the method in strategic management research . Managerial summary : This article illustrates the use of Group-Based Trajectory Models in discerning heterogeneity in an attribute of interest, including firm resources, capabilities, strategies, and performance, especially when such heterogeneity changes or evolves over time. We illustrate these advantages of GBT models in an analysis of how the moderating effect of markets for technology on the value of technological capability is itself moderated by firm types. Specifically, we find that the performance of firms, whose strategic position is based on technological competence, is negatively impacted when MFT are extensive, whereas that of firms whose strategic position is also based on other complementary capabilities is relatively unaffected . summary.oneLiner: When technology can be bought on open markets, firms relying only on technological competence suffer, while firms with complementary capabilities are largely unaffected.
summary.overview: The paper does two things. Substantively, it asks how "markets for technology" (where firms can license or buy technology instead of developing it) change the value of a firm's own technological capability. Methodologically, it introduces group-based trajectory (GBT) models to strategy research: a statistical technique that sorts firms into groups based on how an attribute evolves over time, useful when theory gives little guidance on how firms differ. ISB's research directory describes the setting as a novel dataset of Indian pharmaceutical firms. The authors find that the effect of markets for technology on the value of technological capability itself differs by firm type.
summary.question: Does the effect of markets for technology on the value of technological capability differ across types of firms, and how can group-based trajectory models reveal such heterogeneity when it changes over time?
summary.method: Group-based trajectory models (a finite-mixture method) identify firm types whose attributes evolve differently over time; the authors then examine how markets for technology moderate the link between technological capability and performance for each type. Estimation details are not stated in the available sources.
summary.data: According to ISB's research directory, a novel dataset of Indian pharmaceutical firms. Years and sample size are not stated in the available sources.
findings: Firms whose strategic position rests on technological competence see performance hurt when markets for technology are extensive.
Firms whose position also rests on other complementary capabilities are relatively unaffected.

ISB's summary adds that technological capability generally improves performance and matters more for export-intensive than domestic-oriented firms, with product-innovation capability more valuable for domestic-oriented firms and process-innovation capability more valuable for export-intensive ones.
The authors argue GBT models can uncover heterogeneity in resources, capabilities, strategies and performance when it evolves over time.
summary.whyItMatters: Technical strength alone may be a fragile advantage when technology can be bought; complementary capabilities appear to protect performance. For researchers, the paper offers a way to let the data reveal groups of firms instead of imposing them in advance.
